title: The Savoy Male and Female College
text:
ALEXANDER C. BOHANNON

Alexander C. Bohannon was a Virginian who in the course of a long career as a college teacher had followed the westward development of educational institutions and had been attracted to Savoy by 1881. Some of his earlier life as a teacher is sketched in the following brief biography:

Alexander C. Bohannon, professor at Christian College, Texas, was born in Mathews County, Virginia, July 22, 1820, and was a son of Reuben W. and Nancy Bohannon, both of whom were born in the same place. He Bohanny in 1820. Reuben W. Bohannon was a man of mark in his section; he was a patriot of his country; he held the respect of everybody; was a man of Christian character. Reuben W. was a member of the Christian Church.

Professor Alexander C. Bohannon is the second graduate of Hampden-Sidney, and was raised on the home farm in Virginia. After a preliminary common-school and academic education, and after pursuing a course of seventy studies, Virginia College, then located at Portsmouth, finished his education, when studied with Professor J. A. Cocke, of Virginia. He was, however, compelled him to relinquish his studies, but he soon recovered and studied law with Judge Harris, of Mathews, until 1861. He then taught school until the outbreak of the war, when he enlisted in the Confederate cavalry. He was taken and sometime a prisoner in 1862 he was honorably discharged on account of ill health. He was then occupied in various pursuits, but in 1864 again entered the Confederate service and taught until 1864. The war having come to a close, in company with others, established a high school at Concord, North Carolina, and organized a school, but in 1868 the school was broken up. He continued his teaching.

In 1869 he returned to the place of his birth, and after his father's death left Virginia, and moved to Indiana; then taught at various places; went from there to Hopkinsville, Kentucky, where he was connected with the South Kentucky College. He came to Texas, where he taught at the Christian College, Columbia, Kentucky, and then taught at Sherman, Texas, before accepting the invitation of Professor Holland to fill the chair of logic and rhetoric at the Savoy College, Savoy, Texas.
